previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder managed with a suprapubic catheter, was admitted with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection presenting with high fever, tachycardia, and malaise. He was initially treated with IV vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Urine cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa; due to intermediate sensitivity of Pseudomonas to ciprofloxacin, he was transitioned to high-dose oral ciprofloxacin for a 14-day course per infectious disease guidance. His symptoms resolved, and labs normalized. A suprapubic catheter exchange was performed during admission. He improved to baseline motor function and was discharged home with follow-up arranged in urology and instructions to monitor for recurrence.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure to be part of your care. 

You were admitted to the hospital because you developed symptoms 
concerning for a recurrent urinary tract infection. As you know 
you are at risk for these infections given that you always have 
a foley in place to help you urinate. You received IV 
antibiotics initially and your infection improved. You were 
transitioned to Bactrim prior to discharge.

Additionally you were seen by the speech and swallow team during 
your stay because you endorsed previously know difficulty 
swallowing solid food. They recommended ground food with thin 
liquids.

If you experience any symptoms of worsening infection at home 
(including fevers/chills/weakness) then please seek medical 
attention.

You should follow up with the infectious disease team as an 
outpatient to discuss whether you should be on life long 
antibiotic prophylaxis to try to prevent additional urinary 
tract infections.
